drafts.descriptive: How much does {metric} vary among {stakeholder} with {element}{twist}?
drafts.explanatory: Why did {metric} change for {stakeholder} after {lever} for {element}{twist}?
drafts.evaluative: Did {lever} for {element} lead to {goal} for {stakeholder}{twist}, compared with […]?

realism.label: Data exist
realism.q: Can you name a dataset that measures your metric, at your scale and time step?
realism.evidence: The dataset, its licence and its date
realism.pass: Name it below, with its licence and date.
realism.warn: Look before you commit: find one dataset and open it.
realism.block: As written, the question cannot be answered: change the metric or the scale, or plan to collect data.

realism.label: Physics sanity
realism.q: Do the units and sizes make sense: power in MW against energy in MWh, nothing above its rating, energy in balance?
realism.evidence: One number you checked, with its units
realism.pass: Keep the units on the card.
realism.warn: Check one number with units before you go on.
realism.block: Fix the units or the sizes before anything else.

realism.label: Institutions
realism.q: Can you say who pays, who permits, and which jurisdiction's rules apply, as of which date?
realism.evidence: The rule that applies, and its date
realism.pass: Write the rule and its date below.
realism.warn: Find the tariff, market rule or regulation that applies.
realism.block: A rule can flip the answer: find it first.

realism.label: Scope fits the time
realism.q: Could a first version be done in the research capstone's 20 to 40 hours, or in the time your project has?
realism.pass: Note what a second version would add.
realism.warn: Narrow the scale, the period or the boundary.
realism.block: Cut it to one scale, one period and one metric.

realism.label: People and ethics
realism.q: If people or communities are part of the study, do you know how you will get consent and treat them fairly?
realism.evidence: Your consent plan, or “no people involved”
realism.pass: Keep the plan with the card.
realism.warn: Ask a mentor before you collect anything about people.
realism.block: Plan consent and fair treatment, with a mentor, before any data collection.

crowding.source: OpenAlex, articles and reviews published 2016 to 2 November 2026, keyword search of titles and abstracts (the queries above); retrieved 2 November 2026
crowding.rgi: RGI: growth from 2016–18 to 2022–24, divided by the growth of energy-systems work as a whole (1.70 times). Above 1: faster than the field.
caveats: Context only: the clusters overlap, and the counts are not weighted by quality.
Refreshed yearly with the same queries.
Few papers is no evidence that a question is new, important or feasible.
Many papers is no evidence that it is done.

search.note: OpenAlex accepts AND, OR, quotation marks and brackets; other databases need small changes to the same string.
search.live: Optional: a rerun link opens OpenAlex's current results in a new tab. They change as papers are added, so they differ from the snapshot; note the date you search.
search.noreq: The page itself asks OpenAlex nothing: it searches the dated snapshot.

examples.combo: S1 · society · community solar · low-income renters
examples.question: Did a rural co-op's community-solar programme lower renters' energy burden more than bill credits of the same cost would have?

card.audience: the co-op's board, deciding whether to keep the programme
card.metric: energy burden: yearly energy bills as a share of income

examples.question: How much irrigation pumping on a Plains farm could move to windy night hours without lowering yield, and what is that worth under the co-op's tariff?

card.audience: the farm's owner, who sets the pumping schedule
card.metric: pumping energy moved to windy night hours, and the bill saving it brings

examples.combo: S3 · security · heat pumps · elderly households · cold snap
examples.question: During a week-long cold snap, how would all-electric heating change the risk of losing heat for elderly households, with and without backup?

card.audience: the city's emergency planners, who decide where backup heat goes
card.metric: share of elderly households without heat for more than 12 hours
card.units: % of elderly households, per cold snap

examples.combo: S2 · environment · data-center cooling · nearby communities · drought
examples.question: How do the cooling choices of large data centers shift water use and summer peak demand in a water-stressed region?

card.audience: the region's water utility and grid planner
card.metric: cooling water withdrawn, and the data-center load's summer peak

examples.combo: S4 · security · batteries · regulators · mineral disruption
examples.question: How sensitive is a national storage build-out to a one-year disruption of one mineral, and which design choices reduce the risk?

card.audience: national energy regulators, who set storage targets
card.metric: storage built by 2040, and total system cost, across disruption cases

examples.question: Which productive uses make a solar mini-grid viable without lowering household access?

card.audience: the mini-grid's operator, with the farmers who would buy its power
card.metric: the mini-grid's net present value with each productive use, household supply kept as it is

examples.combo: S3 · avoided demand · building retrofits · city council
examples.question: Why did some neighborhoods' heating demand fall more than others after a retrofit program?

card.audience: the city council, which runs the retrofit program
card.metric: fall in heating demand per home after the retrofit

exemplars.title: Two cards from the same spin
exemplars.task: Spin: S3 city and region · society and livelihoods · heat pumps · low-income renters · a heat wave. Write a question card.

answers.label: Weak answer

parts.note: Help with what? The word hides the metric.

parts:
low-income renters in heat waves?
Type: predictive
Audience:

parts.note: A group, but no use for the answer is stated. Renters could use it; say for what, or name who controls the change.
No units: hours above a safe indoor temperature could be counted.
No falsification statement, so no result could count against it.
No realism review and no closest papers: nobody yet knows whether data exist or what is already known.

answers.label: Strong answer
parts:
Question: During a week-long heat wave, how many hours above the city's indoor-heat threshold would Prairie City's low-income renters avoid if landlords installed heat pumps instead of window air conditioners?
Type: predictive
Audience:

parts.text: the city's housing office, which sets rental standards
parts.note: A user and the use: the office sets the standards the answer informs. Landlords control the installation; that is a separate line.

parts.text: hours above the indoor-heat threshold, per household per heat wave
parts.note: A metric with units, from indoor sensors or a building model.

parts.text: window air conditioners in the same homes
parts.note: A realistic alternative, not “no cooling at all”.

parts: Scale and boundary: S3; renter households in Prairie City;

parts.text: landlords' installation costs left out, and said so
parts.note: The boundary names what it leaves out.

parts.text: heat-pump homes saw no fewer hot hours than homes with window units
parts.note: A result that would show the expectation false.

parts.text: whether renters can afford to run the cooling during the heat wave
parts.note: The uncertainty that could change the answer most, and it comes from the spin's society dimension.

parts.text: 27 °C indoors, the limit in Prairie City's 2026 rental code (fictional)
parts.note: A defined cutoff: the city's own rule, not a universal health standard.

parts.text: warn: the city's sensor panel (illustrative) covers 40 renter homes, too few to split by building type
parts.note: A named dataset, and why it warns.

parts.text: pass: both options are sized at about 3 kW of cooling per flat, so hot hours differ by how they run, not by size
parts.note: One worked check that the comparison is like for like.

parts.text: rules pass (the rental code allows either unit); time pass (one summer of data); people warn (sensors in homes need each household's consent)
parts.note: The other three checks, each with its evidence or the reason for its warning.

parts.text: three found, each differing (owner-occupied homes; a cooler city; cooling bills, not hot hours)
parts.note: How the card differs from each closest paper. The line shows the form of the notes; the papers come from your own searches.
